newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's hardleft rejects calls for mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy's hardleft rejects calls for mini-budget.

text.p: Fausto Bertinotti, leader of Italy's hardline Communist Refoundation party, said he saw no need for a mini-budget next year.

"The 1997 budget is already exhaustive...we have done what we had to do to overhaul state accounts and get ready for the single European currency," said Bertinotti, whose party guarantees the government's parliamentary majority.
The 1997 budget package, which aims to cut 61.5 trillion lire from next year's projected deficit, is currently passing through parliament and must be approved by year end.

But Italian industrialists' group Confindustria said on Monday that an additional mini-budget would be necessary if the government was going to meet its 1997 goals. Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Tuesday he did could not exclude the possibility of fresh financial measures next year.

Bertinotti told a group of foreign reporters that an additional budget risked propelling the country into recession, and added that the government would have little room to manoeuvre if it wanted to bolster accounts further.
"Any action on public spending or taxes would be unacceptable," he warned.
And he said Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left administration would have to reduce the unemployment rate, which is currently running close to 12 percent.
"Next year the government will live or die on its ability to tackle unemployment," he said. "So far it has totally overlooked the problem." -- Crispian Balmer, +396 6782501
